newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks surge; end strong.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks surge; end strong.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average surged in the final minutes of trading Tuesday as investors shifted out of technology stocks and ran to the relative safety of the blue-chip market.
The Dow ended up 51.57 points at 6,858.11, reversing the previous session's loss of 49 points. The Nasdaq Composite index, which is laced with technology stocks, was off 3.83 points at 1,331.51.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,302 to 1,186 on active volume of 480 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

The late rally saw mutual fund traders flock to many of the big-name stocks that have driven the market higher in recent months. Oil shares in particular found support after a weak performance on Monday.
Chevron Corp., Exxon Corp. and Texaco Inc. were all among the Dow's strongest performers.
But the market's real test of confidence took place among technology stocks, which suffered a second straight session of stiff selling pressure.
Late in the day, however, some top names in the sector, notably Intel Corp., finally attracted buyers and traders said the buying interest seemed to spark a rapid-fire turnaround for big-name stocks.
"A lot of people were watching Intel today," said Mike Rothberg, director of portfolio trading at Cantor Fitzgerald.
Intel, the world's largest maker of computer chips is considered a technology bellwether and many analysts use the stock to gauge investor sentiment towards the sector.
Wall Street was nervous after the stock fell early in the session below a key level at 150 and then "dropped like a stone" to 146-1/2, but then, suddenly, the tide turned, Rothberg said.

"Buyers seemed to step in at 146 for Intel and it looked like that flushed out buyers for other large cap stocks," he said. "Before long, we saw buy programmes starting to kick in and those really helped us at the end."
The late surge saw other big technology companies like Microsoft Corp. and International Business Machines Corp. also reverse losses.
By the end, Intel finished at 152, up 1/4 for the day, while Microsoft rose 3/4 to 98-1/2, recouping losses that took it as low as 95-1/8. IBM gained 2-1/2 to 145-1/4 after falling as low as 141-1/8.
Despite the late vote of confidence, investors clearly remained leery of small-name technology stocks as well as any shares whose growth prospects appeared to be in doubt.

Motorola Inc. was one such stock, falling 4 to 63-1/2 after Swedish cellular telephone competitor LM Ericsson said it expected continued pressure on its telecommunications product price levels in 1997.
Motorola made similar comments just a month ago, but even so, investors beat a hasty retreat from the group.
"With the market as nervous as it is, stocks are getting knocked down every time there's bad news," said Barbara Marcin, vice president at Citibank Global Asset Management.

Among individual stocks, Centennial Technologies Inc., whose stock jumped more than fivefold last year, said it was checking the accuracy of previously reported financial statements, and announced that its chief executive officer had been fired. The stock did not open for trading after closing Monday at 16-3/8.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 4.16 points to 789.59. The American Stock Exchange index rose 1.40 to 589.24.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 1.74 to 414.09. The average share was up 18 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,561.243 up 18.498 or 0.25 percent.
